::: {.lesson-meta}
[Level 4 · Models & learning]{.level-4} [⏱ ~100 min]{} [Prerequisites: [Simple regression](38-simple-regression.qmd), [Factors](../01-foundations/06-factors.qmd)]{}
:::

::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- fit a regression with several predictors and interpret each coefficient **holding the others constant**;
- include **categorical predictors**, read their dummy coding and change the reference level;
- fit and visualise an **interaction** between a numeric predictor and a factor;
- diagnose **multicollinearity** (VIF), **influential points** (leverage, Cook's distance) and **heteroscedasticity**, and compute robust standard errors;
- show a model's predictions with a **partial effect plot** and report the model in words.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(broom)
```
:::


## 1. Why more than one predictor?

At the end of [Simple regression](38-simple-regression.qmd) we found that the slope of body mass on flipper length is about 50 g/mm across all penguins, but only about 33 g/mm within Adelie penguins. Gentoo penguins have *both* longer flippers *and* larger bodies, so part of the overall slope is really a **species difference**.

With a single predictor, every other influence is mixed into its slope. **Multiple regression** puts several predictors in the same model, so that each coefficient describes the association of one predictor with the response **after accounting for the others**.

## 2. Two numeric predictors: "holding the others constant"

Fuel efficiency (`mpg`) in the `mtcars` data falls with car weight (`wt`, in 1000 lb). Heavier cars also tend to have more horsepower (`hp`): the correlation between `wt` and `hp` is 0.66.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_wt <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)
m_wt_hp <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

coef(m_wt)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> (Intercept)          wt 
#>      37.285      -5.344
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
coef(m_wt_hp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> (Intercept)          wt          hp 
#>    37.22727    -3.87783    -0.03177
```


:::
:::


The coefficient of `wt` drops from -5.34 to -3.88. They answer different questions:

- **Simple model:** cars that are 1000 lb heavier have, on average, 5.3 fewer mpg — partly because heavier cars also have more powerful engines.
- **Multiple model:** among cars **with the same horsepower**, those that are 1000 lb heavier have, on average, 3.9 fewer mpg.

"Holding horsepower constant" is a statistical adjustment, not an experiment. Nobody added weight to a car while keeping its engine fixed; the model compares cars that differ in weight but have similar horsepower.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
summary(m_wt_hp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> Call:
#> lm(formula = mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
#> 
#> Residuals:
#>    Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
#> -3.941 -1.600 -0.182  1.050  5.854 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept) 37.22727    1.59879   23.28  < 2e-16 ***
#> wt          -3.87783    0.63273   -6.13  1.1e-06 ***
#> hp          -0.03177    0.00903   -3.52   0.0015 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> 
#> Residual standard error: 2.59 on 29 degrees of freedom
#> Multiple R-squared:  0.827,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.815 
#> F-statistic: 69.2 on 2 and 29 DF,  p-value: 9.11e-12
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Each row of the coefficient table tests $H_0: \beta_j = 0$ **given the other predictors in the model**. Both `wt` and `hp` add information beyond the other.
- **Multiple R-squared** is 0.83. Adding a predictor can never decrease R²; **adjusted R²** (0.81) penalises each extra parameter and is fairer for comparing models of different size (more in [Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd)).
- The **F-statistic** now tests all slopes at once: $H_0: \beta_{wt} = \beta_{hp} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: what "adjusting" means (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)

In matrix form $y = X\beta + \varepsilon$, and OLS gives $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$.

The coefficient of `wt` in the multiple model equals the slope obtained by (1) regressing `mpg` on `hp` and keeping the residuals, (2) regressing `wt` on `hp` and keeping the residuals, (3) regressing the first residuals on the second. In words: it is the association between the parts of `mpg` and `wt` that `hp` cannot explain.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
e_mpg <- resid(lm(mpg ~ hp, data = mtcars))
e_wt  <- resid(lm(wt ~ hp, data = mtcars))
coef(lm(e_mpg ~ e_wt))["e_wt"]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   e_wt 
#> -3.878
```


:::
:::


The same number as in `m_wt_hp`.
:::

## 3. Categorical predictors and dummy coding

Now add `species` to the penguin model.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_add <- lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len + species, data = penguins)
tidy(m_add)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#>   term             estimate std.error statistic   p.value
#>   <chr>               <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)      -4031.     584.2      -6.901 2.551e-11
#> 2 flipper_len         40.71     3.071    13.25  1.402e-32
#> 3 speciesChinstrap  -206.5     57.73     -3.577 3.981e- 4
#> 4 speciesGentoo      266.8     95.26      2.801 5.392e- 3
```


:::
:::


A factor with $k$ levels enters the model as $k - 1$ **dummy variables** (0/1 indicators). The first level, here `Adelie`, is the **reference level** and has no dummy of its own. We can see this in the **model matrix**, the numeric table that `lm()` actually uses:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
model.matrix(m_add)[c("1", "161", "302"), ]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     (Intercept) flipper_len speciesChinstrap speciesGentoo
#> 1             1         181                0             0
#> 161           1         209                0             1
#> 302           1         197                1             0
```


:::
:::


Row 1 is an Adelie (both dummies 0), row 161 a Gentoo, row 302 a Chinstrap. (We select rows by their *names*: rows with missing values were dropped, so positions and names no longer coincide.)

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read the coefficients

- `flipper_len`: within a species, 1 mm longer flippers go with 40.7 g more body mass on average — much less than the 49.7 g of the simple model.
- `speciesChinstrap`: Chinstraps are on average 207 g **lighter than Adelies with the same flipper length**.
- `speciesGentoo`: Gentoos are on average 267 g **heavier than Adelies with the same flipper length**.
- The intercept is the expected mass of an Adelie with 0 mm flippers — not meaningful.
:::

Geometrically, the model draws **three parallel lines**, one per species, with a common slope and different heights.

### Changing the reference level

Coefficients of a factor are always *differences from the reference*. To compare with Gentoo instead, change the reference with `relevel()` (base R) or `fct_relevel()` (forcats):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins_g <- penguins |>
  mutate(species = fct_relevel(species, "Gentoo"))

lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len + species, data = penguins_g) |> coef()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      (Intercept)      flipper_len    speciesAdelie speciesChinstrap 
#>         -3764.67            40.71          -266.81          -473.32
```


:::
:::


The fitted values are identical; only the parametrisation (and hence the meaning of each coefficient) changes. To test whether `species` as a whole matters, compare models with and without it (`anova(m_without, m_with)`, see Section 4) rather than looking at single dummies.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: why only $k-1$ dummies?

With an intercept column of 1s and a dummy for *every* level, the dummies sum to the intercept column: the columns of $X$ are linearly dependent and $X^\top X$ cannot be inverted. R would report `NA` for one coefficient ("not defined because of singularities"). Dropping one level (treatment contrasts, R's default) removes the redundancy. Other codings exist (`contr.sum` for effect coding, `contr.poly` for ordered factors) and change the meaning of the coefficients, not the fit.
:::

## 4. Interactions: when slopes differ

The additive model forces the three species to share one slope. Is that reasonable? An **interaction** lets the slope of `flipper_len` depend on `species`. In a formula, `a * b` means `a + b + a:b`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_int <- lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len * species, data = penguins)
tidy(m_int)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   term                          estimate std.error statistic   p.value
#>   <chr>                            <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)                  -2536.      879.5     -2.883  4.188e- 3
#> 2 flipper_len                     32.83      4.627    7.095  7.691e-12
#> 3 speciesChinstrap              -501.4    1523.      -0.3291 7.423e- 1
#> 4 speciesGentoo                -4251.     1427.      -2.979  3.106e- 3
#> 5 flipper_len:speciesChinstrap     1.742     7.856    0.2217 8.247e- 1
#> 6 flipper_len:speciesGentoo       21.79      6.941    3.139  1.843e- 3
```


:::
:::




::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read an interaction

- `flipper_len` is now the slope **for the reference species** (Adelie): 32.8 g/mm.
- `flipper_len:speciesChinstrap` is how much the Chinstrap slope **differs** from the Adelie slope. Chinstrap slope = 32.8 + 1.7 = 34.6 g/mm.
- Gentoo slope = 32.8 + 21.8 = 54.6 g/mm.
- The `species` main effects are now differences in mass **at flipper length 0**: meaningless and huge. Centre the predictor (e.g. `I(flipper_len - 200)`) to make them differences at 200 mm.
:::

Visualise separate slopes by fitting one line per species. With `colour = species`, `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` fits exactly the lines of the interaction model:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_len, body_mass, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Separate regression lines by species (the interaction model). The Gentoo line is steeper.](39-multiple-regression_files/figure-html/fig-interaction-1.png){#fig-interaction fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Is the extra flexibility needed? The additive model is **nested** in the interaction model (it is the special case where both interaction coefficients are 0), so an F-test compares them:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
anova(m_add, m_int)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> Analysis of Variance Table
#> 
#> Model 1: body_mass ~ flipper_len + species
#> Model 2: body_mass ~ flipper_len * species
#>   Res.Df      RSS Df Sum of Sq    F Pr(>F)   
#> 1    338 47666988                            
#> 2    336 46147424  2   1519564 5.53 0.0043 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
```


:::
:::


The p-value (0.0043) suggests that the slopes do differ — mainly because the Gentoo line is steeper. Note that the Chinstrap interaction on its own is far from significant: the overall F-test is the right way to judge "does the interaction matter?".

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: numeric × numeric interactions

With two numeric predictors, `y ~ x1 * x2` gives $\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_1 x_2$, so the slope of $x_1$ is $b_1 + b_3 x_2$: it changes *continuously* with $x_2$. Here $b_1$ is the slope of $x_1$ when $x_2 = 0$, which is why **centring** both variables (subtracting their means) is almost always a good idea before interpreting main effects.
:::

## 5. Multicollinearity and the VIF

When predictors are strongly correlated with each other, the model struggles to separate their effects: the coefficients become **unstable** and their standard errors **inflated**. Consider four correlated car characteristics:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_four <- lm(mpg ~ disp + hp + wt + drat, data = mtcars)
cor(mtcars[, c("disp", "hp", "wt", "drat")]) |> round(2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>       disp    hp    wt  drat
#> disp  1.00  0.79  0.89 -0.71
#> hp    0.79  1.00  0.66 -0.45
#> wt    0.89  0.66  1.00 -0.71
#> drat -0.71 -0.45 -0.71  1.00
```


:::
:::


The **variance inflation factor** of predictor $j$ is $\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)$, where $R_j^2$ is the R² from regressing predictor $j$ on all the *other* predictors. It says how many times larger the variance of $\hat\beta_j$ is than it would be with uncorrelated predictors.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
car::vif(m_four)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  disp    hp    wt  drat 
#> 8.209 2.894 5.097 2.280
```


:::
:::


Let us check one by hand:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
r2_disp <- summary(lm(disp ~ hp + wt + drat, data = mtcars))$r.squared
1 / (1 - r2_disp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 8.209
```


:::
:::


Engine displacement is largely predictable from the other three (R² = 0.88), so its standard error is inflated by a factor of about $\sqrt{8.2} \approx 2.9$. Common rules of thumb flag VIF above 5 or 10.

What to do about it depends on the goal:

- **Prediction**: collinearity does not hurt predictions within the range of the data; you may leave it alone, or use [penalized regression](43-penalized-regression.qmd).
- **Explanation**: you cannot separate effects that the data do not separate. Drop redundant variables, combine them into one index, or accept wide CIs and say so.

For models with factors, `car::vif()` reports a generalized VIF (GVIF) per term, and `GVIF^(1/(2*Df))` is the version comparable to the square root of an ordinary VIF.

## 6. Influential points: leverage and Cook's distance

Some observations pull the fitted model more than others.

- **Leverage** ($h_{ii}$, from `hatvalues()`) measures how unusual an observation's **predictor values** are. High-leverage points *can* move the line a lot.
- **Cook's distance** combines leverage with the size of the residual: it measures how much *all* the fitted values would change if the observation were removed.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cd <- cooks.distance(m_wt_hp)
lev <- hatvalues(m_wt_hp)

tibble::tibble(car = names(cd), cooks_d = cd, leverage = lev) |>
  arrange(desc(cooks_d)) |>
  head(4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   car               cooks_d leverage
#>   <chr>               <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Chrysler Imperial  0.4236  0.1865 
#> 2 Maserati Bora      0.2720  0.3942 
#> 3 Toyota Corolla     0.2084  0.09950
#> 4 Fiat 128           0.1574  0.07991
```


:::
:::


A common screening threshold is $4/n$ (= 0.125 here) for Cook's distance and $2p/n$ for leverage ($p$ = number of coefficients). These are flags, not verdicts.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(m_wt_hp, which = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residuals vs leverage with Cook's distance contours for mpg ~ wt + hp.](39-multiple-regression_files/figure-html/fig-leverage-1.png){#fig-leverage fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


What happens without the most influential car?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
worst <- names(which.max(cd))
worst
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "Chrysler Imperial"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
update(m_wt_hp, data = mtcars[rownames(mtcars) != worst, ]) |> coef()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> (Intercept)          wt          hp 
#>    38.57947    -4.41966    -0.03055
```


:::
:::


The `wt` coefficient moves from -3.88 to -4.42. **Never delete a point just because it is influential.** Check whether it is a data error; if it is genuine, report results with and without it, or use a model that fits it better (here: a curved relationship, see Exercise 5).

## 7. Heteroscedasticity and robust standard errors

The **E** of LINE asks for a constant error variance. When the spread of the residuals changes with the fitted values (**heteroscedasticity**), the coefficients are still unbiased, but the usual standard errors are wrong. A classic example is ozone concentration in New York (`airquality`):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_oz <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind, data = airquality)

augment(m_oz) |>
  ggplot(aes(.fitted, .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Fitted ozone (ppb)", y = "Residual")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residuals vs fitted values for Ozone ~ Temp + Wind: the spread grows with the fitted value (a funnel).](39-multiple-regression_files/figure-html/fig-ozone-1.png){#fig-ozone fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


The **Breusch–Pagan test** asks whether the squared residuals can be predicted from the predictors:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lmtest::bptest(m_oz)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> 	studentized Breusch-Pagan test
#> 
#> data:  m_oz
#> BP = 6.1, df = 2, p-value = 0.05
```


:::
:::


A small p-value is evidence of non-constant variance (the plot is usually more informative than the test). **Heteroscedasticity-consistent ("robust", "sandwich") standard errors** remain valid without assuming constant variance:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lmtest::coeftest(m_oz, vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(m_oz, type = "HC3"))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> t test of coefficients:
#> 
#>             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
#> (Intercept)  -71.033     22.449   -3.16    0.002 ** 
#> Temp           1.840      0.203    9.05  4.9e-15 ***
#> Wind          -3.055      0.907   -3.37    0.001 ** 
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
```


:::
:::


Compare with `tidy(m_oz)`: the estimates are identical, but the robust SE of `Wind` is noticeably larger than the classical one, so the test is less confident. `HC3` is a good default for small and moderate samples. Alternatives: transform the response, or use a model whose variance naturally grows with the mean (a [GLM](42-poisson-regression.qmd)).

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: the sandwich

The classical covariance is $\hat\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}$, which assumes $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2$ for all $i$. The sandwich estimator replaces it with

$$
(X^\top X)^{-1} \Big( \sum_i \omega_i\, x_i x_i^\top \Big) (X^\top X)^{-1},
\qquad \omega_i = \frac{e_i^2}{(1 - h_{ii})^2} \ \text{for HC3},
$$

the "bread–meat–bread" shape that gives it its name. Each observation contributes its own squared residual instead of a common $\hat\sigma^2$.
:::

## 8. Partial effect plots: showing what the model says

A table of coefficients is hard to read once there are interactions. A **partial effect plot** shows the model's predictions as one predictor varies, with the others **held at fixed values**. We do this with `predict()` on a grid.

We add `sex` to the interaction model and plot predicted body mass against flipper length, by species, for **female** penguins:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_full <- lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len * species + sex, data = penguins)
```
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
grid <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(flipper_len)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  reframe(flipper_len = seq(min(flipper_len), max(flipper_len),
                            length.out = 50)) |>
  mutate(sex = factor("female", levels = levels(penguins$sex)))

pred <- predict(m_full, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence")
grid <- bind_cols(grid, as.data.frame(pred))

ggplot(grid, aes(flipper_len, fit, colour = species, fill = species)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Predicted body mass (g)",
       colour = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Predicted body mass of female penguins by flipper length and species, with 95% confidence bands. Each line covers only the observed range of its species.](39-multiple-regression_files/figure-html/fig-partial-1.png){#fig-partial fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Restricting each line to its species' observed range avoids extrapolation. Packages such as **marginaleffects** (`plot_predictions()`) and **ggeffects** automate this, but the logic is always the same: build a grid, predict, plot.

Notice that once `sex` is in the model the species slopes are more similar (`anova(lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len + species + sex, data = penguins), m_full)` gives p ≈ 0.08). Interactions — like any coefficient — depend on what else is in the model.

## 9. Reporting a model

A good report states the model, the sample, the key estimates **with CIs and units**, and how assumptions were checked. For the additive penguin model with sex:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_report <- lm(body_mass ~ flipper_len + species + sex, data = penguins)
tidy(m_report, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   term             estimate conf.low conf.high   p.value
#>   <chr>               <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)       -365.8  -1412.     680.8   4.922e- 1
#> 2 flipper_len         20.02    14.43    25.62  1.155e-11
#> 3 speciesChinstrap   -87.63  -178.8      3.541 5.953e- 2
#> 4 speciesGentoo      836.3    668.7   1004.    4.112e-20
#> 5 sexmale            530.4    456.0    604.8   2.414e-35
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
glance(m_report) |> select(r.squared, sigma, nobs)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   r.squared sigma  nobs
#>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1    0.8669 295.6   333
```


:::
:::




> We modelled body mass (g) as a linear function of flipper length, species and sex (n = 333 penguins with complete data). Holding species and sex constant, each additional millimetre of flipper length was associated with 20 g more body mass (95% CI 14.4 to 25.6). Males were on average 530 g heavier than females of the same species and flipper length (95% CI 456 to 605). The model explained 87% of the variance in body mass; residual plots showed no marked departures from linearity or constant variance.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Interpreting a main effect in the presence of an interaction as "the" effect.** With `x * group`, the coefficient of `x` is the slope in the *reference group* only.
2. **Judging a factor by its individual dummies.** Whether `species` matters is a question for an F-test comparing models, not for one dummy's p-value — which depends on the arbitrary reference level.
3. **"Controlling for" as magic.** Adjustment only removes the confounding of variables you *included*, measured *well*. It does not turn observational data into an experiment.
4. **Deleting influential points to "clean" the data.** Investigate them; report sensitivity analyses.
5. **Including a variable twice.** Two versions of the same information (e.g. a factor and its numeric code, or a variable and its sum with others) cause perfect collinearity and `NA` coefficients.
6. **Reading p-values after looking at many models.** Choosing predictors based on the data makes the reported p-values too optimistic (see [Model selection](40-model-selection.qmd)).
:::

## 10. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. In `lm(mpg ~ wt + hp)`, the coefficient of `hp` is −0.032. Interpret it.

Among cars of the same weight, each additional horsepower is associated with 0.032 fewer mpg on average (about 3.2 fewer mpg per 100 hp).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. A factor `region` has levels North, Centre, South (North is first). How many coefficients does `lm(y ~ region)` estimate, and what does the intercept mean?

Three: the intercept and two dummies. The intercept is the mean of `y` in the North (the reference level); each dummy is the difference between that region's mean and the North's.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. True or false: a predictor with VIF = 12 makes the model's predictions unreliable.

**False**, in general. High VIF inflates the uncertainty of that *coefficient*; predictions for new data similar to the training data can still be accurate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q4. Robust (HC3) standard errors change which part of the output?

Only the standard errors, and hence t values, p-values and CIs. The coefficient estimates and fitted values do not change.
:::

## 11. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — reproduce.** Fit `mpg ~ wt + factor(am)` on `mtcars` (`am`: 0 = automatic, 1 = manual). Interpret the coefficient of `factor(am)1`. Then make "manual" the reference level and refit.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
cars2 <- mtcars |>
  mutate(am = factor(am, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("auto", "manual")))
lm(mpg ~ wt + am, data = cars2) |> tidy(conf.int = TRUE)

cars2 |>
  mutate(am = fct_relevel(am, "manual")) |>
  lm(mpg ~ wt + am, data = _) |>
  coef()
```
Holding weight constant, manual cars have essentially the same mpg as automatics (difference about −0.02, CI from about −3 to 3). The large raw difference in mpg between transmissions is explained by manual cars being lighter. Relevelling only flips the sign of the coefficient.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — interpret an interaction.** From `m_int`, compute by hand the predicted body mass of a Gentoo with 220 mm flippers and of an Adelie with 190 mm flippers. Check with `predict()`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
b <- coef(m_int)
gentoo_220 <- b["(Intercept)"] + b["speciesGentoo"] +
  (b["flipper_len"] + b["flipper_len:speciesGentoo"]) * 220
adelie_190 <- b["(Intercept)"] + b["flipper_len"] * 190
c(gentoo_220, adelie_190)

predict(m_int, data.frame(flipper_len = c(220, 190),
                          species = c("Gentoo", "Adelie")))
```
About 5230 g for the Gentoo and about 3700 g for the Adelie. For a Gentoo you add *both* the Gentoo intercept shift and the Gentoo slope shift.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug.** A student writes

```r
penguins2 <- penguins |>
  mutate(is_adelie = species == "Adelie",
         is_chinstrap = species == "Chinstrap",
         is_gentoo = species == "Gentoo")
lm(body_mass ~ is_adelie + is_chinstrap + is_gentoo, data = penguins2)
```

and gets `NA` for one coefficient. Explain why and give two ways to fix it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The three indicators always sum to 1, which equals the intercept column: the design matrix is singular (Section 3, *Going deeper*). R drops the last one and reports `NA`. Fixes: (1) leave the coding to R with `lm(body_mass ~ species, data = penguins)`; (2) drop one indicator (it becomes the reference); or (3) drop the intercept with `- 1` so that each coefficient is a group mean.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — collinearity in action.** Fit `mpg ~ disp`, then `mpg ~ disp + wt`. What happens to the coefficient and the standard error of `disp`? Compute the VIF of `disp` in the second model by hand.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
tidy(lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars))
tidy(lm(mpg ~ disp + wt, data = mtcars))
1 / (1 - summary(lm(disp ~ wt, data = mtcars))$r.squared)
```
Alone, `disp` has a clearly negative slope (about −0.041, SE about 0.005). Together with `wt` (correlation about 0.89) its slope shrinks to about −0.018, its SE roughly doubles, and it is no longer clearly different from zero. The VIF is about 4.7 (= 1/(1 − 0.89²)). The data cannot tell displacement and weight apart well.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — mini-analysis.** For `mpg ~ wt + hp`, (a) draw the four diagnostic plots; (b) add a quadratic term for weight (`I(wt^2)`) and test whether it improves the fit with `anova()`; (c) does the most influential car (by Cook's distance) remain as influential?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(m_wt_hp); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

m_quad <- lm(mpg ~ wt + I(wt^2) + hp, data = mtcars)
anova(m_wt_hp, m_quad)

sort(cooks.distance(m_wt_hp), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
sort(cooks.distance(m_quad), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
```
The residuals-vs-fitted plot is U-shaped, a sign of curvature. The quadratic term improves the fit clearly (F-test p ≈ 0.004). The Chrysler Imperial, a very heavy car whose mpg the straight-line model underestimates, has the largest Cook's distance (about 0.42) in the linear model; in the quadratic model its Cook's distance drops to about 0.28 because the curve follows it better, and the Maserati Bora (an extreme `hp` value) becomes the most influential car (about 0.31). Influence is a property of a point *and* a model.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `lm(y ~ x1 + x2)` | coefficients adjusted for the other predictors |
| `model.matrix()` | the numeric design matrix (dummies included) |
| `relevel()`, `fct_relevel()` | change the reference level of a factor |
| `y ~ x * group` | interaction: a different slope of `x` per group |
| `anova(m_small, m_big)` | F-test for nested models |
| `car::vif()` | variance inflation factors |
| `hatvalues()`, `cooks.distance()`, `plot(m, which = 5)` | leverage and influence |
| `lmtest::bptest()` | Breusch–Pagan test of constant variance |
| `lmtest::coeftest(m, vcov. = sandwich::vcovHC(m))` | robust standard errors |
| `predict()` on a grid | partial effect plots |

- Each coefficient in a multiple regression is an association **holding the other predictors constant**.
- Factors become $k-1$ dummies; coefficients are **differences from the reference level**.
- With an interaction, the slope of one predictor **depends** on the other; visualise it.
- Diagnose collinearity, influence and non-constant variance — and decide what to do based on whether your goal is explanation or prediction.
